the predominance in the maternal mode of organelle inheritance evolved from relaxed inheritance patterns to avoid the spread of selfish elements.
uniparental organelle inheritance is the result of an evolutionary arms race between selfish cytoplasm and the nuclear genome.

(a) organelle inheritance is not uniparentally transmitted in all species, (b) uniparental transmission is the result of the evolution of mechanisms to prevent the spread of selfish elements, (c) these mechanisms are not absolute, and (d) they are prone to mutational meltdown, which results in fall‐back to sexual recombination.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of organelle genomes.
the mechanisms of organelle inheritance, and the evolutionary forces that have shaped these mechanisms.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the maternal mode of organelle inheritance evolved as an adaptation to avoid the spread of selfish genetic elements, but that this mode of inheritance is not evolutionarily stable and is therefore prone to fall‐back.
uniparental organelle inheritance is the norm, but not the law.
organelle genomes are inherited predominantly from the mother because of a mutational load in sperm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
organelles have a tendency to evolve uniparentally, and when they do, they tend to evolve maternally, because the paternal gamete has a high mutational load.

the maternal mode of organelle inheritance has been selected to prevent the spread of selfish elements, but that this selection is relaxed on short time scales and that the maternal mode is therefore an unstable evolutionary trait.
the evolution of the uniparentally maternal mode of inheritance is the result of a tug‐of‐war between the benefits of sexual recombination and the deleterious effects of selfish cytoplasms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
organelle inheritance is a dynamic and complex trait that is not fixed, but evolves and changes over time.
